objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain how your ELT works and the rules for testing and inspecting it, pick survival gear for the terrain, climate and water you will fly over, and brief passengers on the extinguisher, exits, survival kit, and any parachute or autoland system.
why: After a forced landing, your gear and how fast rescuers find you decide whether everyone survives. Injured survivors lose survival chances fast in the first 24 hours, so planning before takeoff matters.

prereading.what: ELT types, testing, false alarms, search and rescue, flight plans, survival equipment.
prereading.label: AIM 6-2-4 and 6-2-6

prereading.what: Distress calls, actions before a crash landing or ditching, ditching procedures.
prereading.label: AIM 6-3-1 to 6-3-3

warmup: Your airplane goes down in a snowy forest 40 miles from home, and no one is hurt. Nobody knows your route. What three things do you wish you had in the airplane?

key_terms.def: Emergency locator transmitter: a battery-powered beacon that helps searchers find a downed aircraft.
Digital ELT detected by satellite. Can carry owner and position data. Must be registered with NOAA.
Older analog ELTs. Satellites no longer listen for them.
The international satellite system that detects 406 MHz distress beacons.
Rescue Coordination Center (Air Force inland, Coast Guard maritime) that runs search and rescue.
A forced or precautionary landing on water.
Sea surface motion caused by a distant disturbance; land parallel to it, never into its face.
A rocket-deployed parachute that lowers the whole airplane slowly to the ground.
Emergency Autoland: a system that can fly, navigate and land the airplane if the pilot is incapacitated.

chunks.title: ELT: how it works and its limits

body.p: ELTs are required for most general aviation airplanes [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]]. They are battery operated and transmit on 121.5 MHz, 243.0 MHz, or 406 MHz [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]].

head: 121.5 / 243.0 MHz (analog)
406 MHz (digital)
rows: Nearby ATC or an overflying aircraft on 121.5/243.0 [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]]
Satellites; NOAA passes it to an RCC [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]]
Owner info; newer models also position [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]]
Often waits for an overdue report; can take hours [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]]
Includes a low-power 121.5 MHz homing transmitter [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]]

bullets: 406 MHz ELTs must be registered with NOAA [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]].
When armed, it activates automatically from crash forces and transmits for at least 48 hours [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]].
It only helps if it survives the crash and activates [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]]. Pilots and passengers should know how to turn it on manually and check that it is transmitting [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]].
If you fly an airplane with only an analog ELT, consider carrying a 406 MHz personal locator beacon [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].

callout.text: Before engine shutdown after every flight, listen on 121.5 MHz to catch a false ELT activation. If you hear one, check your own ELT and tell the nearest ATC facility [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].

check.q: Why is a 121.5 MHz-only ELT a weak link today?
check.a: Satellites stopped monitoring 121.5/243.0 MHz in 2009, so only nearby ATC or overflying aircraft may hear it, and SAR may wait hours for confirmation [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]] [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].

body.p: 14 CFR 91.207 says most U.S.-registered civil airplanes must have an approved ELT attached, in operable condition [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(a)]]. It must be attached so crash damage to it is unlikely; fixed and deployable automatic ELTs go as far aft as practicable [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(b)]].

head: Rule
Requirement
rows: When the transmitter has been in use for more than 1 cumulative hour, or when 50 percent of the battery's useful life (as set by the ELT maker) has expired. The new expiration date is legibly marked on the outside of the ELT and entered in the maintenance record. The 50 percent rule does not apply to batteries (such as water-activated ones) that are essentially unaffected in storage [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)]]

Within 12 calendar months after the last one: proper installation, battery corrosion, operation of the controls and crash sensor, and a sufficient signal radiated from the antenna [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(d)]]

You may ferry a newly acquired airplane to where an ELT will be installed, or an airplane with an inoperative ELT from a place where it can't be repaired to a place where it can. Only required crewmembers aboard [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(e)]]
ELT temporarily removed (inspection, repair, modification or replacement)

Aircraft records entry (date removed, make, model, serial number, reason) and an "ELT not installed" placard in view of the pilot; no operation more than 90 days after it was first removed [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(f)(10)]]

body.p: Exceptions include training operations conducted entirely within a 50 NM radius of the airport where the local flight began [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(f)(3)]], and aircraft equipped to carry not more than one person [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(f)(9)]].

head: Operational test
How [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]]
rows: Per manufacturer, ideally in a shielded room or test container
Only during the first 5 minutes after any hour, no longer than three audible sweeps; otherwise coordinate with the nearest FAA tower

callout.text: A false ELT alert looks exactly like a real one and can launch a costly search [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].

check.q: Your ELT was used for 70 minutes during a search exercise. What now?
check.a: Replace (or recharge) the battery: it has been in use more than 1 cumulative hour [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)]].

body.p: The current Part 23 airworthiness standards require a way to put out a cabin fire that the pilot can easily reach while seated; level 3 and 4 airplanes must also have one for passengers [[60:112|14 CFR 23.2325(f)]]. Older airplanes were certificated under earlier rules, so check what yours has.

bullets: Know where it is and how it works, and brief passengers (the F in SAFETY) [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]].
In a cabin fire, use the extinguisher first, then open the vents to clear smoke and fumes [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].
If smoke gets worse with vents open, close them; airflow may be feeding the fire [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].
An extinguisher does not stop the source. Shut down the faulty system and land as soon as possible [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].
Ignited materials can keep burning even after power is removed [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

callout.text: On preflight, make sure you can reach the extinguisher from your seat [[60:112|14 CFR 23.2325(f)]]. Its agent, how to use it and its limits come from its label and the POH.

check.q: Fire in the cabin. Vents first or extinguisher first?
check.a: Extinguisher first, then open the vents to purge smoke. Close them if the smoke increases [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

chunks.title: Survival gear for climate and terrain

body.p: For flight over uninhabited land, take survival equipment for the climate and terrain, and know how to use it [[34:35|AIM 6-2-6]]. On remote trips, ask during preflight: is there the right clothing, water, and survival gear on board for a forced landing [[1:48|PHAK 2-9]]?

head: Flying over
What the FAA sources say to carry
rows: Appropriate clothing, water, and survival gear for a forced landing [[1:48|PHAK 2-9]]
Survival equipment for the type of climate and terrain, and know how to use it [[34:35|AIM 6-2-6]]
Effective water survival equipment [[34:35|AIM 6-2-6]]; flotation gear (next chunk)
A working ELT, or a 406 MHz personal locator beacon if the airplane has only an analog ELT [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]]; a flight plan [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6]]

body.p: The ACS adds the target: water, clothing and shelter for 48 to 72 hours (ACS PA.IX.D.R1). Build your list for the season and terrain with your CFI.

**Be easy to find.** After a crash landing, stay with the aircraft unless you have good reason to believe searchers won't find you, and prepare ways to signal search aircraft [[34:47|AIM 6-3-2]]. Use the ground-air visual code. Symbols should be at least 10 feet high, with as much color contrast as possible [[34:36|AIM FIG 6-2-1]].

callout.text: V = need help. X = need medical help. If in doubt: SOS [[34:36|AIM FIG 6-2-1]].

check.q: You are down in a field after a forced landing, uninjured. Stay or walk out?
check.a: Usually stay with the aircraft and get signals ready, unless you have good reason to think searchers won't find you [[34:47|AIM 6-3-2]].

body.p: At sea, survival depends on crew skill in emergency procedures and on good water survival equipment [[34:35|AIM 6-2-6]].

bullets: Rule: when operated for hire over water beyond power-off gliding distance from shore, approved flotation gear must be readily available to each occupant, plus at least one pyrotechnic signaling device (unless under part 121) [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(b)(12)]].
FAA-approved life vests are inflatable. Inflate them AFTER exiting the aircraft. They have a water-activated light [[34:166|AIM 7-6-9]].
Brief passengers on where the vests are and how to use them [[34:166|AIM 7-6-9]].
If you must ditch, try to ditch near a surface vessel; ATC may help find one [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]].

body.p: **Choosing a heading.** Success depends on, in order: sea conditions and wind, type of aircraft, and pilot skill [[34:49|AIM 6-3-3]]. Avoid the face of a swell. Land parallel to the swell, picking the direction with more headwind [[34:50|AIM 6-3-3]].

bullets: Touch down at the lowest speed and sink rate that allow safe handling, nose up [[34:50|AIM 6-3-3]].

Over glassy water or at night it is easy to misjudge height by 50 feet or more; carry enough power to hold 9 to 12 degrees nose up and 10 to 20 percent above stall speed until contact [[34:51|AIM 6-3-3]].
Low-wing: no more than intermediate flaps. Keep a retractable gear up unless the POH says otherwise [[24:356|AFH 18-7]].
An airplane ditched slowly in a normal landing attitude does not sink right away; intact wings and tanks float it for at least several minutes [[24:356|AFH 18-7]].

check.q: You must ditch into a moderate swell with a crosswind. Land into the wind or parallel to the swell?
check.a: Parallel to the swell, accepting crosswind; landing into the face of a swell is dangerous [[34:50|AIM 6-3-3]].

body.p: A ballistic parachute lowers the whole airplane slowly enough that occupants usually survive with minor or no injuries. The airframe is lost [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].

bullets: Catastrophic loss of control from a collision or mechanical failure.
Actual loss of control.
Pilot incapacitation.
Deploy within an acceptable flight regime; follow the manufacturer's guidance [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].
Know how to arm and disarm it before and after flight [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].
Preflight: check the mounts, safety pin and flag, and activation handle and cable [[24:345|AFH 17-11]].
Brief passengers who can reach the handle: when it is safe to deploy (normally only if the pilot is incapacitated) and at least the basic steps [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].
Once on the ground, the deployed parachute and surface winds create hazards. Everyone should know how to evacuate [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].

check.q: When would a passenger pull the parachute handle?
check.a: Generally only if the pilot were incapacitated. The pilot should brief the conditions for a safe deployment and the basic steps [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].

body.p: If EAL senses erratic flying, it stabilizes the airplane and checks whether the pilot responds. With no response it starts an emergency descent, then an automated landing. A pilot or a passenger can also activate it manually [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].

bullets: Broadcasts on the last selected frequency and on 121.5 MHz, and squawks 7700 [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].
Within 12 miles of the runway and at or below 12,000 feet MSL, it broadcasts on tower or CTAF [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].
It picks an airport with an RNAV or GPS approach, preferring towered airports, based on weather, wind and runway length [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].
If GPS is lost, it flies straight ahead until GPS returns [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].

callout.text: EAL cannot see and avoid traffic, follow ATC instructions or NOTAMs, avoid MOAs, restricted areas or TFRs, or turn on aircraft lights [[24:372|AFH 18-23]].

body.p: Brief passengers on when and how to activate it (for example, if you become incapacitated) using the POH.

check.q: Name two things EAL cannot do.
check.a: Any two: detect and avoid other aircraft, follow ATC instructions or NOTAMs, avoid MOAs/SUA/restricted areas/TFRs, turn on lights [[24:372|AFH 18-23]].

chunks.title: Do it step by step: gear, briefing and going down

bullets: 1. Look at the route: terrain, climate, water. Pick gear to match [[34:35|AIM 6-2-6]] [[1:48|PHAK 2-9]].
2. Check the ELT battery date and 12-month inspection, and the extinguisher [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)]] [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(d)]].
3. File a flight plan, or at least tell someone your route and destination [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6]].

4. Brief passengers with SAFETY [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]]: seat belts and harness; air vents; fire extinguisher location and use; exits, evacuation plan, and the survival kit location and contents; traffic; your questions. Add life vests, ELT activation, parachute and autoland if equipped [[34:166|AIM 7-6-9]] [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]] [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].

body.p: **If a crash landing or ditching is coming** [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]]

bullets: 5. MAYDAY call with position, souls on board, ELT status, aircraft color and emergency equipment on board.
6. Turn on the ELT if the installation permits.
7. If fire risk is not a factor, set the radio for continuous transmission.

body.p: **Simulated parachute deployment (if equipped):** say aloud why the situation qualifies, then follow the manufacturer's deployment checklist step by step, touching (not pulling) the handle [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].

head: ACS standard
What the examiner looks for
rows: Identify appropriate equipment and personal gear.
Brief passengers on proper use of on-board emergency equipment and survival gear.
Simulate ballistic parachute deployment procedures, if equipped.

check.q: What does the E in the SAFETY briefing cover?
check.a: Exit doors (how to secure and open), emergency evacuation plan, and the emergency/survival kit location and contents [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]].

chunks.title: Risk: 48 to 72 hours on your own

body.p: The ACS asks you to carry water, clothing and shelter for 48 to 72 hours (ACS PA.IX.D.R1). The AIM shows why:

bullets: An injured survivor's life expectancy can drop as much as 80 percent in the first 24 hours; uninjured survivors' chances fall fast after the first 3 days [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6]].
Without a flight plan, 36 hours normally pass before family concern starts an alert [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6]].
With a VFR flight plan, a search starts if you haven't closed it within one-half hour after your ETA [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6]].
An analog ELT alert may wait hours for confirmation [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].

body.p: **Parachute and autoland risks.** A ballistic parachute saves lives when deployed within an acceptable flight regime, so you must understand the deployment conditions before flight [[24:371|AFH 18-22]]. Hesitating to save the airplane is a known trap [[24:351|AFH 18-2]]. Autoland cannot avoid traffic or airspace [[24:372|AFH 18-23]]; it relies on its radio broadcasts and a 7700 squawk to alert ATC and other pilots [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].

callout.text: Flight plan + 406 MHz beacon + 72 hours of water, warmth and shelter = found alive.

check.q: Why can a flight plan matter more than the survival kit?
check.a: It starts the search within one-half hour after your ETA; without one, 36 hours normally pass before family raise the alarm [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6]].

bullets: Skipping the passenger briefing on the extinguisher, exits and survival kit [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]].
Storing the survival kit where you can't reach it after a crash; keep it in one reachable container [[34:166|AIM 7-6-9]].
Inflating a life vest inside the cabin [[34:166|AIM 7-6-9]].
Testing an analog ELT outside the first 5 minutes after the hour without coordinating with the nearest FAA tower, or testing it in the air [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].
Not checking the ELT battery expiration date [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)]].
Not knowing the arming, disarming and deployment steps for the parachute system [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].
Walking away from the airplane after a forced landing [[34:47|AIM 6-3-2]].

check.q: When do you inflate an approved life vest?

scenario.title: Mountain trip in a parachute-equipped airplane
scenario.setup: In late fall you plan a 2-hour VFR flight over forested mountains with two passengers, in an airplane with a ballistic parachute and a 406 MHz ELT. The forecast is clear, so a passenger says you don't need the winter gear or a flight plan; it will only add weight.

questions.q: Do you leave the gear and skip the flight plan?
questions.a: No. For uninhabited terrain, carry survival gear for the climate and terrain [[34:35|AIM 6-2-6]], and plan water, clothing and shelter for 48 to 72 hours (ACS PA.IX.D.R1). A flight plan starts a search within one-half hour after your ETA; without one, 36 hours normally pass [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6]].

questions.q: What do you brief the passenger next to the parachute handle?
questions.a: The conditions for a safe deployment (normally only if you are incapacitated) and the basic deployment steps [[24:371|AFH 18-22]], plus SAFETY items like the extinguisher and survival kit [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]].

questions.q: Over the ridges, the engine loses oil pressure and quits. There is no field, only tall trees. When is the parachute the right choice?
questions.a: The AFH names catastrophic loss of control, actual loss of control and pilot incapacitation as qualifying conditions, and says deploy within an acceptable flight regime [[24:371|AFH 18-22]]. For a forced landing over trees, follow the manufacturer's guidance, which you studied before flight. A desire to save the airplane must not delay the decision [[24:351|AFH 18-2]].

questions.q: Before touchdown, what radio and ELT actions help rescuers?
questions.a: MAYDAY with position, people on board, ELT status, aircraft color and emergency equipment; turn on the ELT if the installation permits [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]].

skills.do: Tell the examiner what emergency equipment is on the airplane (ELT, extinguisher, parachute or autoland if equipped) and what personal and survival gear you would carry for the route's terrain, climate and water.
skills.practice: For three routes (desert, mountains in winter, over a large lake), write a gear list and justify each item. Check the ELT battery date and inspection on your airplane [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)]].

skills.do: Give a full passenger briefing on belts, exits, extinguisher, survival kit, ELT, and life vests if carried.
skills.practice: Brief a friend using the SAFETY list [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]] until you can do it in under two minutes without notes.

skills.do: If the airplane has a ballistic parachute, say when you would use it and touch-through the deployment checklist.
skills.practice: Study the manufacturer's material [[24:371|AFH 18-22]]; practice the deployment flow on the ground with the safety pin installed.

quiz.q: An ELT battery must be replaced (or recharged) when:
options: Every 24 calendar months, whether or not it has ever been used or tested
Used for over 1 cumulative hour, or 50 percent of its useful life expired
After any test of the ELT, even a brief one on the ground in the proper window
Only when it fails the 12-calendar-month ELT inspection or fails a self-test
quiz.why: Either condition triggers replacement or recharge [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)]].

quiz.q: How often must a required ELT be inspected?
options: Every 100 hours of flight time on the airplane
Before each flight, as part of the preflight check
Every 24 calendar months from the last inspection
Within 12 calendar months of the last inspection

quiz.q: An analog 121.5 MHz ELT may be tested on the ground:
options: At any time of day, for up to one minute with the antenna connected
Only in flight, once you are high enough that nobody on the ground hears it
During the first 5 minutes after any hour, no more than three sweeps
Only at night, when few other aircraft are listening on 121.5 MHz

quiz.q: Which ELT is detected by satellites today?
options: All three
406 MHz
quiz.why: Satellite monitoring of 121.5/243.0 MHz stopped in 2009 [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]] [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].

quiz.q: Which flight does NOT need an ELT under 91.207?
options: A training flight kept within 50 NM of the departure airport
A cross-country flight of 90 NM in a four-seat airplane
A night flight carrying passengers to another airport
A flight over water well beyond gliding distance of the shore

quiz.q: When ditching in a swell, you should:
options: Land parallel to the swell, avoiding its face
Land on the face of the swell, into its rising slope
Always land directly into the wind, whatever the swell
Land with full flaps in a low-wing airplane
quiz.why: Avoid the face of a swell; land parallel to it [[34:50|AIM 6-3-3]].

quiz.q: A passenger should normally pull the ballistic parachute handle:
options: Whenever the engine runs rough
Never; only the pilot may
On every forced landing
Only if the pilot is incapacitated
quiz.why: Generally the passenger deploys only if the pilot is incapacitated [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].

options: Avoid TFRs and restricted areas
Squawk 7700 and broadcast on 121.5 MHz
Follow ATC instructions
See and avoid other traffic
quiz.why: It broadcasts on the last frequency and 121.5 MHz and squawks 7700; it cannot avoid traffic or airspace or follow ATC [[24:371|AFH 18-22]] [[24:372|AFH 18-23]].

takeaways: 406 MHz ELTs are seen by satellite; register them. 121.5 MHz alone is weak.
ELT battery: over 1 cumulative hour or 50 percent life. Inspect every 12 calendar months.
Carry water, clothing and shelter for 48 to 72 hours for the terrain and climate; file a flight plan.
Ditch parallel to the swell; inflate life vests outside the airplane.
Brief passengers with SAFETY, plus ELT, vests, parachute and autoland if equipped.
Decide before flight when you would pull the parachute.
cfi_notes: Have the student find the ELT battery expiration date and last inspection in the logbooks; examiners often ask.

Students confuse ELT exceptions: the 50 NM exception covers only training operations that stay entirely within 50 NM of the airport where they began, not a cross-country that goes farther [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(f)(3)]].
Make students give the SAFETY briefing on every lesson with a passenger or observer.
In parachute-equipped airplanes, rehearse the deploy decision with scenarios (midair, control failure, incapacitation).
Point out that the AIM survival content is general; help students build a kit list for local terrain and season.
gaps: Fire extinguisher types, agents, operating technique and limits (e.g., toxic fumes in a closed cabin) are not covered in these resources; use the extinguisher label and POH.

Specific survival kit contents for hot, cold and mountainous terrain, and amounts of water and food for 48 to 72 hours, are not listed in these resources; the climate table gives general examples only.
Ballistic parachute deployment steps, speed and altitude limits, and EAL activation and passenger briefing details are manufacturer/POH specific.
ACS Appendix 3 (referenced in the Task notes) is not in these resources.

activities.title: Old ELT or new ELT?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap the ELT type it belongs to.

items.t: Satellites stopped listening for it in 2009
Heard only by nearby ATC or an aircraft flying over
Can send owner info, and on newer models, position
Search and rescue may wait hours for an overdue report
Search and rescue can start in minutes

cards.s: An ELT that has transmitted for a total of 45 minutes needs a new battery for that reason alone.
cards.why: No. The use trigger is more than 1 cumulative hour. The other trigger is 50 percent of the battery's useful life [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)]].

cards.s: After a battery change, the new expiration date goes on the outside of the ELT and in the maintenance record.
cards.why: Yes. It must be legibly marked on the outside of the transmitter and entered in the maintenance record [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)]].

cards.s: You may test an analog ELT in flight if you keep it to three sweeps.
cards.why: No. Airborne tests are not authorized. The three-sweep limit is for ground tests [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].

cards.s: A required ELT must be inspected within 12 calendar months after its last inspection.
cards.why: Yes. The inspection covers installation, battery corrosion, the controls and crash sensor, and the antenna signal [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(d)]].

cards.s: When you ferry an airplane with a broken ELT to a repair shop, you may take a friend along.
cards.why: No. Only required crewmembers may be aboard on a ferry flight under this rule [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(e)]].

cards.s: With a records entry and an "ELT not installed" placard, you may fly while the ELT is out for repair, but not more than 90 days after it was first removed.

activities.title: Ditching, step by step
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the ditching steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Before takeoff, brief passengers on where the life vests are and how to use them
Size up the sea and pick a heading parallel to the swell
Turn to the ditching heading and start down
Touch down as slowly as possible, nose up

activities.title: Spell out the SAFETY briefing
activities.intro: Tap a letter, then what you brief for it.

pairs.r: Seat belts, shoulder harness, seat locked in place
Air vents and other cabin controls
Fire extinguisher: where it is and how it works
Exit doors, evacuation plan, survival kit
Traffic: scan, spot, tell the pilot; quiet at busy times

final_quiz.q: Your ELT maker gives the battery a useful life of 6 years. The ELT has never been used. When must the battery be replaced (or recharged)?
options: When the full 6 years of life are used up
Only if it fails a test during an inspection
Every 12 calendar months, at the ELT inspection
When 3 years of its useful life have passed
final_quiz.why: The battery must be replaced when 50 percent of its useful life has expired: half of 6 years is 3 years [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)]].

final_quiz.q: Which of these is NOT part of the required 12-month ELT inspection?
options: A test flight to confirm satellites can hear it
Checking the battery for any corrosion damage
Operation of the controls and crash sensor
Checking that it is properly installed in the airplane
final_quiz.why: The inspection covers installation, battery corrosion, the controls and crash sensor, and the signal from the antenna [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(d)]]. Airborne ELT tests are not authorized [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].

final_quiz.q: You rent an airplane for a trip over remote country and find it has only a 121.5 MHz ELT. What does the AIM suggest?
options: Switch the ELT to 243.0 MHz so satellites can hear it
Test the ELT in flight before you leave the area
Carry a 406 MHz personal locator beacon
Nothing; satellites still pick up 121.5 MHz
final_quiz.why: Satellites stopped monitoring 121.5 and 243.0 MHz in 2009. Pilots who don't own the airplane should check its ELT and, as appropriate, get a 406 MHz personal locator beacon [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].

final_quiz.q: Your ELT was removed for repair 40 days ago. The records entry is made and an "ELT not installed" placard is in view. May you fly?
options: No, never without an ELT
Yes, until 90 days after it was first removed
Yes, but only within 50 NM of your home airport
Yes, but only for 30 days
final_quiz.why: With the records entry and placard, you may operate until 90 days after the ELT was first removed [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(f)(10)]]. The 50 NM exception is a different rule, for local training flights [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(f)(3)]].

final_quiz.q: You smell burning insulation and see smoke in the cabin. You use the extinguisher, then open the cabin vents, and the smoke gets thicker. What next?
options: Close the vents right away
Open the vents wider to clear it faster
Turn the cabin heat on full
Lower full flaps to slow down
final_quiz.why: If smoke increases when the vents are opened, close them at once. More airflow may be feeding the fire, or it may be in the heating system [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

final_quiz.q: Under the current Part 23 standards, where must the means to put out a cabin fire be?
options: In the baggage compartment, behind the rear seats
Outside the cabin, in a compartment next to the door
Next to the ELT in the tail, for ready access in a crash
Where the pilot can easily reach it while seated
final_quiz.why: There must be a means to put out a cabin fire that the pilot can easily reach while seated [[60:112|14 CFR 23.2325(f)]].

final_quiz.q: After a forced landing, one passenger is hurt and needs a doctor. Which ground-air code symbol do you lay out?
options: V
X
N
Y
final_quiz.why: X means require medical assistance. V means require assistance, N means no, and Y means yes. Make it at least 10 feet high [[34:36|AIM FIG 6-2-1]].

final_quiz.q: You filed a VFR flight plan with an ETA of 1500. You go down at 1410 and can't call anyone. When would a search normally start?
options: About 1530, if you haven't closed or reported
At 1500, the moment you miss your filed ETA by a minute
About 1430, thirty minutes after you went down
About 36 hours after 1500 if no one reports you
final_quiz.why: If you fail to respond within one-half hour after your ETA, a search starts [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6]]. The 36 hours is what normally passes with no flight plan [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6]].

final_quiz.q: You must ditch. The swell crests run north and south, so headings 360 and 180 are parallel to the swell. Wind is from 330 at 15 knots. Which heading is best?
options: 330, straight into the wind
180, parallel to the swell
360, parallel to the swell
090, across the swell
final_quiz.why: Land parallel to the swell, and of the two parallel headings pick the one with more headwind [[34:50|AIM 6-3-3]]. 360 has the wind 30 degrees off the nose; 180 has a tailwind. Landing into the wind without regard to the swell can be very dangerous [[34:50|AIM 6-3-3]].

final_quiz.q: When does 14 CFR 91.205 require approved flotation gear for each occupant?
options: On any flight over water that is more than a mile from the shoreline
At night, on any flight over water, even within gliding distance
When for hire, over water beyond power-off gliding distance of shore
On any flight that goes more than 50 NM from the nearest shore
final_quiz.why: The rule applies to aircraft operated for hire over water beyond power-off gliding distance from shore, and also requires at least one pyrotechnic signaling device [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(b)(12)]].

final_quiz.q: A midair collision jams your controls and you can't control the airplane. It has a ballistic parachute. What does the AFH say?
options: This qualifies; deploy within an acceptable flight regime
Try to save the airplane first, since deployment loses the airframe
Deploy only after a passenger agrees and the engine is shut down
Wait until the engine quits or the airspeed decays before you deploy
final_quiz.why: Catastrophic loss of control from a collision qualifies. Deploy within an acceptable flight regime [[24:371|AFH 18-22]]. The desire to save the airplane is a known trap [[24:351|AFH 18-2]].

final_quiz.q: Which statement about Emergency Autoland (EAL) is true?
options: It flies around TFRs and restricted areas
It picks only airports that have an RNAV or GPS approach
It follows ATC instructions sent by radio
It turns on the landing lights before touchdown
final_quiz.why: EAL only considers airports with an RNAV or GPS approach [[24:371|AFH 18-22]]. It cannot avoid TFRs or restricted areas, follow ATC instructions or turn on lights [[24:372|AFH 18-23]].

final_quiz.q: A crash landing is coming. Besides the usual MAYDAY items, which extra detail does the AIM suggest you give to help searchers?
options: Your total flight hours
The date of your last flight review
Aircraft color and emergency equipment on board
Your home airport's phone number
final_quiz.why: With a crash landing or ditching imminent, add items such as ELT status, visible landmarks, aircraft color, people on board and emergency equipment on board [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]].
